#6816. Justin Theroux Took Me on a Nearly Perfect Trip to Japan. Here’s the Itinerary.

“There’s tourism, and there’s travel,” the actor says. After four days across Tokyo and Kyoto, he reveals exactly what that means.

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

Justin Theroux carefully holds the brush perpendicular to the sheet of paper. For the last twenty-odd minutes, he’s been learning how to press, glide, press a single Japanese kanji character: 永, eternity.

The fifty-five-year-old actor has been practicing each one methodically, including a particularly tricky “airplane” maneuver in which he must hold the brush outward, away from his chest, and guide it gently across the sheet to make a tail that broadens as it travels before ending on a punctuating point at which he must deftly lift his hand away.

Despite praise from his instructor, a renowned Japanese calligrapher called Mamimozi—“Sugoi!” she exclaims, which means amazing—Theroux groans at his subpar airplane attempts. He’s not satisfied with good enough, especially now that the stakes have heightened: He’s been handed a thicker sheet that, once it’s inked with 永, will be framed as a gift to take back home to New York after this trip to Japan.

On this particular journey, he’s partnered with the Luxury Collection, a wide portfolio of award-winning hotels and resorts like the Gritti Palace in Venice, or the Royal Hawaiian in Honolulu, to curate experiences like this calligraphy session as a gateway beyond Japan’s typical touristy activities.

“I always feel bad when you see your buses pull up to places, and you see people file out, they take pictures, then they get back on the bus, and they go somewhere else,” he tells Esquire. “Anytime you can get access behind walls to a place—that’s what truly unlocks any travel experience.”

The actor has visited Japan numerous times, and over the course of those visits, has connected deeply with Japanese culture. As a “global explorer” and face of the Luxury Collection Expeditions campaign, Theroux has shaped those life-changing travel experiences into two itineraries.

First, there’s the Global Explorer Edit: Tokyo with Justin Theroux, based out of the five-star Prince Gallery Tokyo Kioicho hotel, which offers panoramic views of Mount Fuji when the weather’s right. If travelers want to branch out beyond Tokyo to Japan’s imperial capital, the Global Explorer Edit: Kyoto with Justin Theroux offers a different perspective of the Land of the Rising Sun. Guests stay at Hotel the Mitsui, a Michelin three-key accommodation, where modern comforts and historic sensibilities collide for a beyond memorable stay.

There’s a noticeable theme to Theroux’s itineraries, visible even in the mundane experience of day-to-day Japan. Everyone here, from the citizen on the street to the service worker to the artist, aims to do their very best, much like Theroux does as he makes his first attempt at 永 on the thicker sheet. The streets are litter-free, despite—or because of—the lack of public garbage cans, and the public transit is perpetually, impeccably, on time.

Though Theroux fails to land the airplane this time, there are a few more sheets lying around, a few more chances to try again—and afterward, a few more stops along his itinerary.

It’s late morning on a partly cloudy September Saturday when Theroux and company—press, PR, friends, guides—leave the Prince Gallery for a speakeasy hidden on the third story of a nondescript building in Tokyo’s Shibuya district. The calligraphy experience awaits inside.

After Theroux decides on his best 永 to frame, Mamimozi, the artist, prepares to perform. She steadies a brush as big as her forearm before making decisive motions, quickly and smoothly, across a sheet the size of a side table. Her movement is entrancing, engrossing—and then, snap, it’s over.

“How does she decide she’s pleased?” Theroux asks Mamimozi’s translator, who passes the question on.

Normally, Mamimozi would do 100 of these before she decides on the best one, the translator relays. This particular character, though? She’s about “92 percent” happy.

“If I ever get to 100 percent,” Mamimozi says through the translator, “that’s the end of my pursuit.” She’s always trying to grow as an artist.

Theroux is presented with his calligraphy in a sturdy frame. For Mamimozi to have taught Theroux from this particular kanji—永, eternity—suddenly makes a whole lot of sense. “I approach everything artistically, whether it’s writing or acting, as a monastic experience where you’re never going to be completely pleased with everything you do—but you’re always striving for something,” he tells Esquire.

The next pursuit? Scoring fashionable vintage wear, of which Tokyo supplies in high volume. Theroux’s Tokyo Edit ensures that travelers are able to take advantage of the spoils of one of the world’s premier fashion markets, focused on four of his favorite shops: Portration, Visvim, Old Joe, and Brackets, all in close proximity in Shibuya. Theroux and co. then attend the Nanzuka contemporary art gallery, also in Shibuya, but travelers should expect a visit on the earlier side of their itinerary.

If shopping makes guests hungry, Theroux’s itinerary recommends Yoroniku, an omakase that serves world-class wagyu. But on this particular trip, Theroux and co. first head to Bar Centifolia, where “samurai bartender” Yuzo Komai puts on a show that’s earned him the title of world’s best cocktail artist.

When an order for a smoked old fashioned is received, the house lights go down, leaving a spotlight on Komai. He unleashes a big blue fan and blows air on a large, perfectly clear ice cube to sweat it just a little before unsheathing a katana and chopping it into a trapezoidal prism, which he slides neatly into a rocks glass. Next he pours in a sweet tincture and Beyoncé’s signature SirDavis whiskey and stirs them together with a cocktail spoon. Then, he places a circular cut of wood atop and lights the whole damn thing aflame with a blowtorch.

A billow of smoke arises from the concoction, which tastes of sweet and smoky caramelized popcorn. For those less adventurous, the bar owns dozens of rare Japanese whiskies, so delicate and floral and complex that they make the perfect nightcap to relax the shoulders after a dizzying, rewarding day.

To begin the Kyoto itinerary, Theroux finds himself sitting cross-legged in the home studio of third-generation lacquerer Nishimura Keikou. His bowls and cups—which go for $650 a pop—begin their lives as a base of wood whittled to a thickness of less than a millimeter before he begins to layer lacquer, a brownish sap that’s extracted from the tree of the same name. It’s a precious resource, “like the blood of a human,” Keikou says through a translator. The trees do not give much, and once depleted, they die. A single piece of lacquerware can take an entire year to craft, as each of the requisite fourteen layers must dry completely before another can be shellacked over top.

Unlike Mamimozi, the calligrapher, Keikou doesn’t consider himself an artist. He doesn’t create because he has an innate need to express; he creates because clients request his goods. Theroux feels a connection nonetheless, especially when Keikou mentions the plight of the woodworkers who make the base of his pieces. They’re behind the camera, so to speak, receiving little glory or credit. Theroux, who is not just an actor but a writer, seems to internalize this as Keikou hands him a bowl as a gift.

Next up on Theroux’s Kyoto itinerary: sushi. His preferred spot, Otachidokoro Sushi Ki, is a stand-up joint where guests can order à la carte or in a set menu. Guests are encouraged to eat with their hands here, which they can rinse between bites using spouts of water that trickle from below a raised edge on the sushi bar.

Theroux’s sushi artisan, befuddlingly, is an Italian immigrant from just outside Milan. How the hell did he get here?

“I came here by plane,” Francesco jokes. Seven years ago, at twenty-seven years old, he committed himself to making sushi at its highest level. Where to go to complete his training? Kyoto, of course, without a return ticket. Now, he’s serving Justin Theroux scallop over soy sauce-soaked rice with a sprinkle of salt and a zest of lime on top.

Bellies full, it’s time for a Zen garden tour. Kyoto is home to many temples and shrines and gardens of both Buddhist and Shinto origin, Japan’s two national religions. But this garden—situated in the Konchi-in Buddhist temple and named, simply, the Crane and Turtle Garden after the shapes of its central rock formations—doesn’t get much foot traffic. It’s more peaceful than the bigger, more popular, tourist-mobbed shrines, ideal for a thoughtful traveler like Theroux.

It’s probably “97 out of 100” in terms of popularity, says tour guide Andrew William. Like the sushi chef from earlier, William is not from Japan. He is from Maryland, not too far from Washington, D.C., where Theroux grew up. Like Francesco, he uprooted himself to perfect his art elsewhere, though instead of making sushi, he designs and builds gardens. He’s worked on big projects in the past, including Ben Stiller’s estate on the north shore of Kauai, Hawaii. William’s pursuit, however, belies the reality of chasing dreams: they often turn to nightmares.

William once wanted to be head groundskeeper of this idyllic garden. But it’s not so easy for foreigners to rise in Japanese hierarchies. He claims to have suffered abuse at the hands of his employers and endured long working hours for low pay—“a lot of bad things to maintain beauty,” he says, still apparently chewing on the irony.

Theroux is no stranger to that feeling. Sometimes, he says of acting, “... you’ll have a miserable experience that’s received very well. And you think, God, I was so miserable on that job. And yet the product was so good, cause so many craftsmen are bringing their talents to bear on it. The editor really helped it, the music really helped it, the director was very good—although they might have been an asshole.”

Theroux and William sit side by side on a broad wooden step that leads into the temple and overlook the amorphous stony shapes of the crane and the turtle. He and Theroux are perched, William says, on what Buddhist philosophy considers the ship of life. Out directly in front of them is an expanse of pebbles raked into a motif of alternating swirls and straight lines, an ocean of respective rough and smooth seas. On the other side, the crane and turtle await, representing the harmony that anticipates us at the end of our earthly journey.

There is still an evening of activities to go: A visit to the temple. Matcha and handmade sweets in the temple’s tearoom. An intimate geisha dinner complete with drinks, cultural conversation, and traditional Japanese food. All of which prove to be enriching experiences for travelers. Yet it is here, facing the crane and turtle, where visitors can meditate on their journey and appreciate the unique experience on which they’ve embarked.

“There’s tourism, and there’s travel,” Theroux says. “And I think they are two totally different things.”

Tourism is hoofing it from place to place, checking boxes. Seen that, did this. But travel, Theroux’s travel, is different. It’s about meeting people, making friends beside the worker at the front desk or the technician at the spa, and engaging with their lives, their realities, on a deeper level.

“Anytime you can have access to something unique or an area of interest—whether that’s craftsmanship, arts, music, dance, knives, enamel ware, things like that—you’re always going to get a little peek into a country or city that you didn’t know existed,” he says.

Like all his endeavors, Theroux’s Japan Expeditions aren’t perfect—if they were, there’d be no reason for visitors to come back—but they’re as close to perfect as it gets.

Both of Justin Theroux’s Tokyo and Kyoto Global Explorer Edits are available for booking on the Luxury Collection Expeditions website. The Tokyo Edit is a day-long experience that costs $9,505, while the Kyoto Edit, also a day-long experience, costs $13,145. That price includes a guest, a one-night hotel stay, a private guide, and transportation.

#6812. The 6 Smartphones to Buy in 2026

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

We don’t care if you’re on team Apple or Android. We’ve found you the phone to upgrade to.

You’ve landed here, so let me guess: You’re an iPhone person and you want a new iPhone. Or ... you’re an Android person, dedicated to your brand of choice already, be it Google or Samsung. Here’s the thing: Your choice of phone says a lot about you, but realistically you’ve already locked yourself into choosing between the same three phones all your friends are getting. We are humans, so our brains are finely tuned to love habits. The result is not too many people want to adjust to a new way of interfacing with daily life every other year; they just want the same thing. There’s a chance you are the rare third kind of person who wants a change. In all three cases, there’s good news. You kinda already know what you want (and don’t want) out of a smartphone.

My fellow editors and I have tried the latest in what Apple, Samsung, and Google have to offer, and have determined for ourselves which are the greatest. This year, the biggest shake-up to the race is foldable phones. Not entirely a new category, but the iPhone Duo is the capstone on a past 12 months that have legitimized the form across both Apple and Android devices. You’ll be paying a premium, and not all the software is properly optimized yet, but the tech is finally there. For everyone else, there’s still the new pro model iPhone or the latest A series Pixel for the value hunters. Regardless of whether you’re after a bold reinvention, or just an improved camera and a slightly shinier display, you’ll find something to love in these six smartphones.

I’ve made vocal arguments in favor of going against the grain and getting a Windows device instead of a MacBook, but at the end of the day it’s all too easy to stick with it if you’re on team iPhone already. The 18 Pro is the iPhone to get if you’re a daily power user, on your phone 24/7 for both work and personal reasons. It’s got a glorious 120-hertz-refresh-rate retina screen, exactly the smoothness and crispness you’ve come to expect from a pro level phone.

It’s not merely the one we’ve seen the most in the wild, it’s the best bet for an iPhone that will last you another four years. And while we can't say we love the new design, it’s been easy to get used to. And functionally, it’s the iPhone Pro we know and love. It is fast, it’s got a smooth 120 hertz screen and it has one of the best cameras you can get on a phone. If there’s one upgrade we truly feel each time we get a new phone, it’s the camera. This year’s is no exception.

Compared with the other Android offerings out there, the Pixel 11 Pro is in elite territory. It’s not technically as beefy as a Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra or ZFold 8 Ultra, but it’s notably a lot cheaper than either of those phones.

It’s fast and it’s got that smooth refresh rate a high-end phone should. Best of all, holy shit is the camera something else? It can take one incredible photo after another and it’s probably equipped with the best selfie camera on a phone. Our editors who’ve tested this one also won’t shut up about how much better Gemini is than every other AI assistant. Finally, a “smart” feature that lives up to the moniker. And compared to the equivalent iPhones and Samsung phones, the battery life reigns supreme—even if, as a trade-off, it takes the longest to charge.

If you’re of the Android persuasion, it’s easy to see the iPhone 18 Pro as the other team’s Google Pixel 11 Pro, instead of the other way around. On a pure specs level it’s a better phone—just probably not better enough to get Apple diehards over the OS gap. Serious sarcasm aside, it’s not the iPhone users who need this phone. It’s everyone currently suffering on an older Pixel model or, worse, some no-name Android phone.

It was only a couple of years ago you could read me advising you not to buy a renewed iPhone. But with how expensive all technology has become recently, there is now a wide enough gulf between something like this and a new iPhone to make buying refurbished worth the cost savings. Instead of buying a 17e new for $700, pick up this refurbished 16e—it’s half the price, and you won’t be living too far in the past.

The 16e is pretty much everything a phone should be and nothing extraneous. This phone is light, yet durable. It’s got the Action Button from the 16 lineup but does lack the Camera Control.

The other omission of note is the lack of MagSafe functionality. The 16e supports wireless Qi charging, but it does not magnetize the way every iPhone since the 12 (barring the SE line) has. Once again, we don’t think this matters to the core audience for this phone, so it’s less of a flaw and more of a way Apple has honed in on exactly the audience it wants to hit for this one.

For $600, this is the most affordable big-name smartphone. There are plenty of Androids in the $200 to $300 range, but by and large they aren’t meant to last. They are poorly made stopgaps to get you to something like the Pixel 10a. Right now for only $400, this is the best value you can get on a brand-new smartphone.

It has a lot of what we love from the newest Pixel phones—including the latest OS features like Gemini and the invaluable Call Screening feature that automatically detects spam. And while the front-facing camera isn’t mind-blowing compared with the 10 series Pixels, it does still rock a very impressive wide-angle back camera that offers more variation than the e series of iPhones.

The iPhone Duo is the most innovative and groundbreaking phone release of the year. We said as much in our gadget awards and editor Luke Gullory has been giving his updates along the way. He’s tested and tested, and the verdict is in. This one is a keeper and, most importantly, it’s the best foldable phone to hit the market yet.

The genius touch here is the aspect ratio. For the Duo, Apple went with a √2:1 (or 1.414:1) aspect ratio. That is slightly different from the other foldable, but the subtle change makes a difference. On the Duo, the small outside screen exactly mirrors the size of half the large inner screen, but it also exactly mirrors the total aspect ratio of the entire large inner screen. The matte screen seems odd at first, but it’s the solution Apple has found to showing any creasing and, once again, this gives it that design edge. There’s a reason people start to care when Apple does it.

I’ll also note it has the same chipset and specs as the 18 Pro, including RAM. Normally, this would put it on par power-wise, but the real-world performance lags behind due to the amount of thermal throttling needed to pull off the design miracle of the form factor.

If you want a flip phone, you can shop vintage for pennies but when it comes to using those like daily phones, the truth is they don’t support modern cellular networks. They are as good as a toy. But if you still want that flip phone experience, Samsung’s most affordable new folding phone gives you something of the sort.

Don’t get me wrong, the Z Flip8 is still expensive, starting at $1,200. But compared to all the other foldables from Samsung and Google, it is technically the least expensive one. That’s largely because it’s got the least amount of screen space. Really it’s just a normal-sized Galaxy phone with a front-screen, not something that has a unique aspect ratio like the Duo or the Galaxy Z Fold 8 phones. On a specs level, it’s on par with these phones. Crisp 120 hertz screen, solid front and rear cameras, and all the Android app support you’d want. Really, though, if you’re committing it’s a commitment to having a wacky, folding flip phone that you can set up like a tent or show off all the different camera modes.

#6807. Artist Kent Monkman’s Latest Work Is Filled With Fashion Easter Eggs

When, four years ago, the Frick Collection invited the Indigenous artist Kent Monkman to create a series of new works, Monkman turned his attention to one of the museum’s smallest—yet most cherished—holdings: Johannes Vermeer’s Officer and a Laughing Girl. The painting, from 1657, depicts a young woman in conversation with an officer wearing a wide-brimmed black beaver hat.

“Beavers used to drive the economy of North America,” says Monkman, who is Cree. “They were the first currency—you paid for things with beaver pelts.”

His wheels soon began to turn. In his practice, Monkman likes to rewrite European art and history from an Indigenous perspective. Could he give this Vermeer a Native twist, with a bit of his signature sense of humor?

The answers to that question make up “Kent Monkman: Officer and Laughing Girl,” on view in the Frick Collection’s Cabinet Gallery from now through February.

In his new acrylic paintings, Monkman replaces the female figure in Vermeer’s original scene with his genderfluid alter-ego, Miss Chief Eagle Testickle, a frequent presence in his work. “Miss Chief has always been in strategic relationships with colonial men,” Monkman says. “She’s always trying to improve the life of her people. She is someone that stands up, talks back, reverses the gaze, and questions authority—and she always does it in a way that is with love. She’s always trying to seduce people with love.”

Over four years, Monkman and his studio created five different versions of Officer and a Laughing Girl using his Miss Chief character. (At the Frick, they’re all set against beaver-themed toile wallpaper.) Not only do both Miss Chief and the officer’s clothes evolve from one painting to the next, but their setting shifts, too, reflecting different elements of Indigenous history. “Through these paintings, I knew I could have a conversation about colonial history, fur trade, treaty relationships, geography, and the dispossession of land,” Monkman says.

There is a deliberate chronology to the paintings. As visitors move clockwise around the space, the works’ colors shift from cool to warm, signaling the growing threat of climate change. There are other references, too. In the first painting—titled New Amsterdam, 1600s—Miss Chief is dressed in a traditional winter coat and a pearl earring (an homage to the Vermeer), talking to the officer in front of a wall-hung hide. In the next, titled New France, 1700s, Miss Chief is seen in trade-silver jewelry, alluding to the currency of that period. “[Fashion] and jewelry really became part of the storytelling, giving clues to the time and the place,” Monkman says.

Elsewhere, in Black Hills, 1800s, a framed portrait of the Lakota chief Sitting Bull, known for defending his tribal lands, is mounted behind the two figures; and in Reservation, 1900s, there is a large map of the nation’s Native reservations at the time: “I was thinking about that period of dispossession and institutionalization of Indigenous peoples.” (Crosses and prison keys also feature in the work.)

As the tones grow warmer—and both Miss Chief and the officer appear in less and less clothing—red emerges as a theme. “It’s always been her signature color,” says Monkman, “but over time, it’s also [represented] this solidarity with missing and murdered Indigenous women.” (Red is the official color of the MMIW movement.)

In Manhattan, 2000s, Monkman works in a reference to modern Indigenous creativity: Miss Chief wears a striking silver cuff by Adrian Standing Elk Pinnecoose, a Diné and Southern Ute artist. “Adrian’s work, to me, represents tradition and futurism,” says Monkman. “I wanted to feature that piece because it’s about where we come from, but also where we are going.”

So, too, is Monkman’s show more broadly, in fact. “I want people to see that we still have joy, and we still have these values that inform how we live with other people, and how we exist in treaty relationships with everyone,” he says. “I wanted Miss Chief to really represent that. And she’s going to bring as much joy, humor, sass, good fashion, and as much sexiness as she can bring.”

#6803. How Does Diplo Survive a Weekend Running, DJing, and Partying? His Whoop Data Tells the Story.

The 47-year-old DJ shared his health stats from a frenzied weekend that could’ve killed any normal person. Here’s how he does it without coming apart at the seams.

On a Saturday morning in August, at exactly 10 a.m., August Thomas Wesley Pentz, the DJ known as Diplo, stood outside the Barlume Beach Club in Montauk, Long Island and delivered a sermon to hundreds of runners. “I'm very tired; I slept three hours for you guys,” he shouted through a megaphone, dressed in grey cargo shorts, a tank top, and pink aviator shades. “But now we're ready to run. Let's have a good time.”

Then one of the world’s most prolific DJs launched himself into a 5K through the sand and rocks of Gin Beach. It was a run club event organized by A Team, a dating app for the wellness-obsessed, and Diplo's Run Club, which stages nine group runs across the U.S. (and soon, Europe).

As I watched him that sunny and hot morning, I couldn’t stop thinking: how the hell is this guy still standing, let alone leading a run? It was only Saturday, and Diplo was already deep into a frenzied weekend. He landed in New York City on Thursday morning after taking the overnight flight from his home in Malibu. That evening he DJ’d from 12:30 A.M. to 3 A.M. at the Edge, a venue 100 floors above the city. On Friday, he boarded a seaplane for the Hamptons, where he performed two more sets: a sunset show at Surf Lodge, where Jimmy Buffett and Snoop Dogg have played to crowds of models and billionaires, followed by an impromptu set at Mary Lou's, a Montauk club on the harbor where he’d only meant to hang out but ended up taking the decks. He didn't leave until around 1 a.m.

I was at both venues and felt deeply, existentially hungover the next morning. I figured—hoped, really—the run would include some walking. Diplo, however, led the pack. He wore a Whoop, the health tracker with which he has a partnership, and reached a heart rate of 167 beats per minute. “He wasn't taking it easy at all,” said Greg Grosicki, a staff research scientist at Whoop who reviewed Diplo’s data from his weekend in Montauk.

I didn't understand how a 47-year-old pulled off this feat—the travel, the DJ sets, the cavorting, the running—without collapsing and retreating to his hotel suite for the rest of the weekend. On Saturday evening he had two more sets, one at the annual gala of the Surfrider Foundation, which supports ocean conservation and includes Sean McPherson and John Slattery as supporters. After that he DJ’d a private party for investment executive Michael Dorrell before flying private to Ibiza overnight for his next gig.

After the run—which, miraculously, I did finish—I talked with Diplo about how he survives this lifestyle. He even shared his Whoop data with me from the weekend so I could compare his body’s reaction with how he told me he felt. “I'm actually fully cracked out every day, doing way more than running and DJing, more than anybody else,” he said.

He likes to sound nonchalant about it. “When I did an interview with some of the Whoop counselors, they were like, your body is very similar mentally to a Navy SEAL or an ER nurse. You're able to just get up and go do whatever,” he said. “I can always get up and get shit done, unless I'm sick.” OK, so maybe Diplo was just born with it. But I learned that he does more for his physical and mental health than he likes to let on. This is the story of how a 47-year-old, internationally renowned DJ, who works and parties into the pre-dawn hours, travels the world, and leads packs of people on runs, pulls it off without coming apart at the seams.

Running appeals to him because it travels well. All you need is a pair of shoes and the will to put them on. “I do things I can do anywhere,” he said. “Running is free.” He aims for 15 miles a week across three or four runs, averaging a seven-and-a-half to eight-minute mile. His fastest mile, six and a half minutes, came after his run club appeared on the prediction platform Polymarket, where people bet against him. “That's what motivated me to run pretty fast,” he said with a laugh.

DJing counts as cardio, too. After all, his sets typically run at least two hours. “It's a mix of dancing and standing,” he said. “It's almost like a little air squat.” He's baffled that his dancers, several from the group Major Lazer, stay in shape without a gym. “I'm like, ‘What do you guys do?’” he said. “They're like, ‘We don't do anything. We just dance at your shows.’"

The numbers back him up: during his Surf Lodge set, his max heart rate hit 117 bpm. “If you consider these sets are two hours long, maintaining a heart rate of 120 is a real physical activity,” Greg Grosicki, the research scientist at Whoop, told me. “It's equivalent to riding a bike for two hours. You feel pretty wrecked after that, and he's getting equivalent strain from his sets.”

Diplo mixes cardio and weights in HIIT sessions and does 100 to 200 push-ups a day, several times a week, usually in his hotel room. “It takes five minutes of your life,” he said.

Once a week he wears an electrical muscle stimulation, or EMS, suit for 20 minutes. “It does pulsing with simple moves,” he said, naming a brand called Catalyst and a newer one, Pepper, he's about to try. He credits the suit, half-jokingly, for his arm muscles.

He also takes hot Pilates classes with light weights and works out at Barry's Bootcamp near his home in Malibu. “There's an unwritten rule about group fitness in California: you don't bother celebrities,” he said. “You let them get their job done, then you tell people you saw Chris Martin. Every time I go to Pilates, he's next to me.”

According to the data, long flights, especially red eyes, hit Diplo hard, said Grosicki. After an overnight flight to Ibiza, Diplo's recovery score—a measure of how ready the body is to perform—dropped to 21 percent, and his sleep score to 29 percent. That’s well below average for him. “He's human, and he's responding to these stressors,” Grosicki said.

“I do like to get the red eyes, which probably messes up my sleep the most, but I'd rather be outside in the day,” Diplo said. “Being on a plane during the day is so depressing.” He said he struggles to hold a circadian rhythm and sometimes crashes mid-afternoon. On Thursday, for example, he slept five hours in the middle of the day ahead of his set at the Edge.

Winding down after a set is its own challenge. “I might take a Xanax if I have to,” he said. “I got to stop thinking about things.” He also puts his phone away, listens to audiobooks and history podcasts, skips food before bed (though he does chug electrolytes), and uses PEMF mats, which send low-frequency electromagnetic waves through the body to aid in relaxation. Mostly, though, he just takes what sleep he can get.

Saturday morning, after two Friday-night sets in Montauk, his recovery score was 67 percent and his sleep score 65 percent, both above average. On Monday, after he spent the night in Ibiza, his recovery score was 56 percent and sleep was 62 percent. As Grosicki put it, “He bounces back.”

Diplo avoids drinking before shows and on travel days and hasn't done recreational drugs in six months. When he does, it's acid. “I would run on acid, just try things on acid,” he said. “I could fly a plane on acid.”

“Mental health is pretty much everything,” Diplo said. “But you have to get there sometimes by exercising. Finding your body, being in tune with your body, is probably the first thing you can do to have a clear mind, to get rid of any sickness you have, whatever's keeping you down. That's the first way to start.”

He's tried more unconventional resets, too. Seven years ago, he smoked toad venom. “I'll never do it again, but it was pretty hardcore,” he said. “It's a really big ego death. Being humbled is very good wellness.”

Whatever he's doing, it seems to be working, at least by the numbers. Whether the rest of us should try it is a different question entirely.

#6800. Madewell and The Six Bells Bring Storybook Charm to the Holidays

The Hudson Valley inn lends its old-world touch to the brand.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

There’s nothing quite like the holiday season to boost your sense of nostalgia for cozy moments at home—especially when they involve a touch of cold-weather whimsy. Whether you’re sipping on a hot coffee or tea as you watch the changing leaves or you’re curled up next to a warm fireplace with your latest read, the colder months of the year are primed for ample charm. Of course, these moments are not without their accoutrements, which is right where the new Madewell collaboration with The Six Bells—a country inn located in the Hudson Valley—comes in.

The Six Bells Inn, founded by Audrey Gelman, features interiors inspired by the imagined English village known as Barrow’s Green—complete with its own fictional characters and landmarks—giving the space an old-world touch that feels as if it’s been plucked right out of a storybook. It’s this distinct aesthetic, along with Gelman’s way of storytelling, that led to the inn’s collaboration with Madewell.

“Steven [Cateron, Madewell’s creative director,] and the team at Madewell understood our little world at Six Bells from the very first conversation we had. In the early stages of working together on this collaboration, we wanted this collection to feel like stepping through a doorway into another time where things feel a little more enchanted,” Gelman told ELLE.com in an email. “Every piece in the collection was designed to have that sense of wonder. We hope it brings the spirit of The Six Bells into people’s lives and homes this holiday season.”

With a range of apparel, accessories, and home décor—including vintage-inspired needlepoint ornaments and pillows, stockings, and toiletry bags featuring custom prints based on the inn’s interiors—the collection combines Madewell’s laid-back style with The Six Bells’s country charm. “For the first time, we’re really leaning into home accents, which let us extend [the Madewell] world beyond what you wear and into the spaces you live in,” Cateron said in an email. “The inn’s wallpapers and patterns were a huge source of inspiration, and you’ll find bits of them throughout the collection, right down to the lining of our Denim Trucker Jacket.” There are also pajama sets and even a nightgown for those who want to take one of summer’s biggest trends straight into the holiday season. And with prices ranging from $17 to $248, there are plenty of pieces ready for the gift-giving season (and no doubt, whoever receives these will be tickled to unwrap them).

The limited-edition, 23-piece collection officially launches on November 12 at 10 a.m.; however, ELLE.com readers have exclusive access to the collection now. Shop the collection below.

#6799. The Saga of Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s Fake Leather Jacket

The internet loved his outrageous new look. There was just one problem.

There are several ways to respond when you've admitted to an affair, your company's shares are tumbling, and even the White House is discussing your private life. Turning up in a spectacularly studded Saint Laurent leather jacket is one of them. Resigning is another.

For a while, it seemed like Jensen Huang, the 63-year-old former CEO of Nvidia, had opted for the former. A photograph showing the tech billionaire in an archival Hedi Slimane YSL biker jacket went viral this week. The internet was delighted. There was just one problem: The photograph was fake.

The resignation, which came just this morning, was real.

As CNN reported, the image had been doctored from a genuine photograph taken at a Seoul airport in June. Nvidia, which one might imagine has other things to deal with right now, confirmed it wasn't real.

But perhaps the reason so many people believed it was that Huang already dresses like this. Leather jackets are his uniform. He reportedly owns 30 or 40 of them, including a snazzy reptile-effect number worn to deliver his company's keynote at the Consumer Electronics Show.

And Hedi Slimane was the perfect designer to bring into the fantasy. The Frenchman, who ran Saint Laurent from 2012 to 2016, made his name dressing skinny rock stars and turning their disheveled, devil-may-care attitude—later rebranded as so-called “indie sleaze”—into expensive luxury fashion. His leather jackets were practically a uniform for men who were determined to look as though they didn't care what anyone thought and/or having a midlife crisis.

For a billionaire in the middle of a spectacularly public scandal, it was quite a look. One Instagram commenter described Huang as the first person to achieve "negative aura" in archival Hedi.

There's another irony. Huang has previously said his wife Lori—i.e., the wronged party in all this—helps choose his clothes.

And then there's the technology itself. Nvidia makes the chips that power the AI revolution, including the tools capable of ... producing convincing fake photographs.

In conclusion then, the image wasn't real. But as a portrait of a billionaire in the middle of a spectacularly public crisis, we so wanted it to be.

#6795. The 17 Best Comedy Movies of 2026

Thanks to The Invite, Coyote vs. Acme, and Stop! That! Train!, big-screen comedy is making a comeback.

Are comedies making a comeback? Over the past decade, you couldn’t get a laugh into theaters even if it was forced. Hollywood decided that comedies weren’t worth the same treatment as superhero tentpoles or low-budget horror, and just about every legacy franchise sequel of a former ‘90s comedy disappointed audiences because they were basically cash grabs that played on nostalgia. Comedy needed help.

So, in 2026, some fresh films forced Hollywood to come to its senses. Coyote vs. Acme, a Looney Tunes film that Warner Bros. originally dropped to claim a tax write-off, grossed over $126 million at the box office. Olivia Wilde’s The Invite might just receive nominations for every major award category at the Oscars, and Airplane!-esque humor made a comeback in RuPaul’s hilarious disaster flick Stop! That! Train!

If you’re in need of a belly laugh, check out the best comedies of 2026 below.

Don’t get me wrong, Coyote vs. Acme is no Space Jam. But the Looney Tunes film that triumphantly won the box office—even after Warner Bros. gave up on it—is still one of the funniest movies of the year. The story follows Wile E. Coyote as he partners with a lowly injury attorney (Will Forte) to sue the ACME Corporation for its defective products. The comedy also stars John Cena as ACME’s defense attorney, who probably has the funniest line of the year when he tells Tweety Bird: “I don’t pay you to tink you taw, I pay you to taw.”

Olivia Colman stars in this romantic comedy drama about a lonely fisherwoman who grows tired of the town’s harassment due to her smell. So, she asks a magical basket weaver (Peter Dinklage) to make her a husband (Alexander Skarsgård) out of wicker. What follows is a bizarre yet hilarious story about the follies of marriage, jealousy, and tons of sex with a man made out of basket material.

Sam Rockwell leads this sci-fi comedy by former Pirates of the Caribbean director Gore Verbinski, about a time-traveler who travels to the same diner over and over again in a Groundhog Day–esque loop because he believes that if he can take the right configuration of people from the diner back to the future with him then he may be able to save the world from AI’s takeover. I know, it’s strange. But Verbinski makes the comedy work, especially when you learn about each diner patron via small vignettes emphasizing various doomsday scenarios.

Real estate agent Rudd Landy (John Cena) is called to the hospital when his brother gets into a car accident. Turns out, the man in emergency care is not his real brother (Christopher Meloni), but someone that he used to mentor when he was younger as part of a Big Brothers Big Sisters program. Without anywhere else to go, Rudd agrees to help take care of his “little brother” (Eric André) while he recovers, even if his little brother might just ruin his life.

When Gail Daughtry’s (Zoey Deutch) husband takes their celebrity sex pass joke literally, Gail sets out to get even by tracking down her celebrity sex pass—John Hamm—to have sex with him and even out the score. The comedy film also stars “Weird Al” Yankovic, Ben Wang, Sabrina Impacciatore, Joe Lo Truglio, Fred Melamed, and Mad Men’s John Slattery as himself.

Johnny Knoxville, Steve-O, and the whole Jackass crew return for one last ride in Jackass: Best and Last, another compilation of skits, stunts, and pranks from some of the most fearless people on the planet. They hit each other in the groin with wooden mallets, hook their penises up to shock collars, and reminisce about some of their most iconic sketches throughout the years.

Half RuPaul’s Drag Race, half Airplane! for Bravo fans, Stop! That! Train! is the dumbest movie I’ve seen all year (complimentary). The film follows RuPaul and her Drag Race stars as they attempt to stop a speeding bullet train heading straight toward the storm of the century, aka a Stormaganza. Even if you’re so out of your depth that you have no idea what’s going on, Stop! That! Train! argues that that’s okay. It’s comedy for comedy’s sake, and we need more of that at the theater.

Mel Brooks just turned 100 years old (!!!). But before that, he was 99 in Mel Brooks: The 99-Year-Old Man!—a two-part HBO documentary directed by Judd Apatow. The film, which chronicles the comedian’s career throughout The Producers, Blazing Saddles, Spaceballs, Young Frankenstein, and many more, also touches on his work as a film producer. Still, it’s the testimonies from his friendship with Carl Reiner and his marriage to Anne Bancroft that really pull at the heartstrings after a good laugh down memory lane.

Olivia Wilde is not afraid of Virginia Woolf. In the actress’s latest film, The Invite, the classic dinner-party setup full of playful talking and relationship arguments somehow morphs into a sex comedy. The whole film takes place in Angela (Wilde) and Joe’s (Seth Rogen) apartment as they welcome the raucous upstairs neighbors Pina (Penelope Cruz) and Hawk (Edward Norton). But unlike Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf? and its descent into anger and grief, The Invite asks more questions about love, commitment, and everyone’s stance on orgies.

The struggling music duo always works for me. Whether it’s Flight of the Conchords or Ishtar, there’s something funny about people with no talent still trying to make it to the top. Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie takes the genre to maybe its lowest budget yet, as the Canadian web-series comedians somehow also make room to spoof Back to the Future and incorporate real Nathan Fielder–like guerrilla filmmaking.

One of the coolest movies to premiere out of SXSW was the Hulu original Mike & Nick & Nick & Alice, from writer/director BenDavid Grabinski. A loan shark (Vince Vaughn) uses a time machine to undo one bad night involving his close friend (James Marsden) and his wife (Eiza González). Mike & Nick & Nick & Alice is the kind of movie you want when the pizza is hot, the beers are cold, and your friends are indecisive about what you all want to watch.

After years of creative and financial slump, Pixar has found its groove again with Hoppers. Essentially Animal Farm meets Avatar, Hoppers tells the story of a genius college student whose participation in a breakthrough science experiment lets her become a beaver who can communicate with animals. Though her efforts to help animals seem promising at first, she quickly realizes what really happens when animals (and bugs!) fight back against mankind. Directed by We Bare Bears creator Daniel Chong, Hoppers is an easygoing, family-friendly romp through the wilderness.

Liam Neeson continues his funny streak in the action comedy Cold Storage. Joe Keery (Stranger Things) plays a slacker employee of a storage facility who, along with his cute coworker (Georgina Campbell), discovers a deadly, mutating fungus. Teaming up with a grizzled federal agent (Neeson), the three work to save the world. Basically a modern-day Outbreak, Cold Storage isn’t one to leave dormant on your watch list.

Dave Bautista and Jason Momoa make up the ultimate action-movie tag team in The Wrecking Crew. The guys play estranged brothers in Hawaii who work together to piece together who killed their father and how on earth the Japanese yakuza is involved.

Boots Riley, the writer and director of Sorry to Bother You, does it again with his crime caper I Love Boosters. In this anticapitalist satire, a crew of professional thieves works to take down a ruthless fashion giant (Demi Moore). Keke Palmer, Naomi Ackie, Taylour Paige, Poppy Liu, Eiza González, and more make up this delirious ensemble that takes Ocean’s Eleven and dresses it in hyper-surreal shades.

Sometimes we need a nauseatingly cute rom-com. Kevin James (yes, The King of Queens) stars in this breezy and uplifting comedy about a man who, after being left at the altar, goes on his Italian honeymoon solo. While there, he makes new friends and even deeper connections with strangers halfway around the world. A feel-good flick about new beginnings, Solo Mio can lift you high when you’re feeling down.

A stoner comedy? In 2026? In this economy? Well, the streaming generation can finally know what it’s like to have their own Harold & Kumar with Pizza Movie. Gaten Matarazzo and Sean Giambrone star as college roommates and social pariahs who, while high on a new hallucinogenic drug, embark on a psychedelic odyssey to make it downstairs and get their pizza delivery. Despite a popular meme mocking the movie’s marketing, Pizza Movie performed well with critics at its SXSW premiere.

#6791. This Olympic Volleyball Player’s Kona Village Wedding Was a Heartfelt Tribute to His Hawaiian Roots

As two UCLA volleyball players, Susannah Muno and Micah Ma’a often crossed paths. “The athlete community at UCLA was pretty tight-knit, so we ran into each other here and there. But we were never really in the same circles,” says Susannah, who goes by Zana. It wasn’t until a dare during their senior year that they truly connected. “I remember so vividly being on the bus with my team during a road trip when I got an Instagram DM from Micah. I screamed,” she says. “Naturally, I passed my phone around to the entire team, and then we all screamed.” It turns out that Micah and two teammates each chose someone for the others to DM. “Very college,” laughs Zana. “Three girls on our team got DMs from three guys on the men’s team that day. Two of those three couples are still together.”

Micah’s friends clearly put fate into motion. Zana and Micah made plans to see each other and that first night, they talked, laughed, and even cried until morning. “Somewhere in the middle of that night, I realized that how hot he was was actually the least interesting thing about him,” says Zana. “I won’t go so far as to say it was love at first sight. But I do think that from that first day together, we both knew there wasn’t really a version of our lives where we didn’t want the other person in it.”

Over the next six years, the two navigated a long-distance relationship as they competed professionally around the world. Micah even represented the United States at the 2024 Paris Olympics and helped the Indoor Volleyball team win a bronze medal. Two weeks later, on August 19th, 2024, Micah proposed. “We drove our little golf cart to dinner at a restaurant in our beach town that I had been wanting to try all summer,” recalls Zana. “After dinner, we went for a walk along the beach, as we often do, and that’s when it happened!” The couple celebrated at home together in their “own little bubble of happiness.” Family and friends helped them pull together an engagement party in just a few days to celebrate. “The very next day, Micah and I packed our bags and left for his next season abroad—a pretty fitting start to the next chapter of our lives,” she says.

The couple decided to tie the knot on May 24, 2026, in Kona Village on the Big Island of Hawai’i. “Micah is Native Hawaiian, and his Hawaiian culture is something deeply rooted within him and his family,” explains Zana. “Having the privilege of getting married on the island of Hawaiʻi, on land that feels so raw, untouched, and sacred, was something we didn’t take lightly. Throughout the entire planning process, we wanted to honor and respect the culture of this land and its people. We kept coming back to one simple vision for the wedding: a sense of place.”

Curating a thoughtful group of vendors made this dream come to life. Alison Rose Events managed planning, while the bride and her future sister-in-law helped lead the design process. “I spent so much time finding the right people—people who felt like family and, in many cases, actually were,” says Zana. “Each of our musicians was a friend of the family, which made every space feel that much more intimate. It wasn’t a stranger playing a violin; it was a friend sharing his gift with us on one of the most meaningful days of our lives.”

Florals, in particular, were a key part of their wedding weekend’s vision. Ren MacDonald-Balasia of Renko Floral foraged greenery and blooms from all over the island—including some family members’ backyards—to create organic arrangements that felt true to the environment. Lei worn throughout the weekend were also hand-made by Micah’s family. “None of these details were about creating something simply for the sake of beauty,” says Zana. “They were about making the weekend feel like us and, just as importantly, making it feel like Hawaiʻi.”

With a full weekend of celebration planned throughout Kona Village, the couple needed to fill their wardrobes with the perfect pieces for each event. Zana looked back in her closet for her first bridal look. “Micah and I actually got legally married the year before at Kona Village with just the two of us and our officiant,” says the bride. “I wore a Hanne Bloch two-piece silk tulle set, and we stood barefoot on the lanai of our hale as we said our vows. When it came time to choose what I would wear to our welcome party exactly one year later, it felt only right to wear that same outfit again.” The groom also donned a piece from the past for the party, choosing to wear his Tūtū’s (grandfather’s) aloha shirt as a nostalgic touch.

The next day was full of activities, starting with a pickleball tournament with a Wimbledon white dress code. The bride wore a matching Alo set and popped on a custom hat the couple had made for all their guests. “Of course, Micah won,” says Zana. “I’m still not sure his partner touched a single ball, but that’s beside the point.” The couple then spent the afternoon poolside with all their guests. Zana kept it carefree in a Monday Swimwear bikini with a Solaqua cover-up. “We had fresh coconuts filled with a little rum float, lounged around the pool, and eventually ended up taking one huge group swim out to the lily pad in the ocean,” she says.

The bride’s next ensemble made a bigger statement. “For our rehearsal dinner, I wore a shell-and-fringe dress by British designer Kilentar that weighed 22 pounds,” Zana says. “The dress was everything that night was: fun, organic, flirty, and a little unexpected. It floated and moved so beautifully, and with literally every step I took, the shells made the most incredible sound.” Micah complemented her natural-toned look in a custom linen button-down and trousers.

Zana at first struggled to find a dress for the wedding day until Danielle Frankel opened her bridal boutique in Los Angeles. “I tried on my dress just days after it had come down the runway, and immediately, my mind was made up,” she says of her strapless gown. “The organic, lightweight linen fabric mirrored the textures of the landscape around us, while the bubble hem gave the dress this beautiful shape and movement that reminded me of the ocean and the lava rock.” Micah had one request for Zana’s bridal ensemble: he asked her to wear a veil. A style from Danielle Frankel was the perfect fit. “I loved it so much that I vowed to myself she will be worn again,” she says.

For Micah’s walk down the aisle, he had a bespoke suit made at The Imperial Tailoring Company in Moscow. “He had been away for the eight months leading up to the wedding, so having a suit made together in the U.S. simply wasn’t possible,” explains Zana. “Instead, we set out to find the best tailor we could in Russia and ended up creating the most incredible custom suit for him.” She adds, “In a funny way, even his wedding look became a reflection of the life we were living at the time.”

During the reception, Zana had two outfit changes. First, she wore a mini dress that was crafted from the skirt of her mother’s wedding dress. “Wearing a piece of my mother’s dress was so much more emotional than I anticipated,” she reflects. Her final look was an Elce linen two-piece set with a backless halter top and pants. “It was very me—comfortable, freeing, and effortless,” Zana says.

Zana’s jewelry throughout the weekend was actually all pieces borrowed from her mother’s best friend, Lisa Wehrly, whom the bride sees as a mentor and role model. “I was able to wear pieces from her collection throughout the celebrations, each one carrying its own stories and history,” she says.

The celebrations kicked off on Friday night with a casual welcome event overlooking the ocean. Cocktails, bites, and conversation led to an unexpected turn. “In classic Hawaiian get-together fashion, it wasn’t long before someone picked up a microphone,” says Zana. “Micah’s sister, Mehana Maʻa, took the mic for a few songs, followed by Micah himself, who sang ‘I’m Yours’ by Jason Mraz. He then somehow transitioned into a hilarious, completely off-the-cuff freestyle, welcoming everyone to this beautiful place and telling them to get ready for the best weekend. Everyone absolutely erupted. It was spontaneous and so perfectly Micah, and it immediately set the tone for the weekend.”

The next day was filled with pickleball, poolside drinks, and connection under the Hawaiian sun. Then, the night turned more intimate with a rehearsal dinner in a Kiawe grove with an open-air barbecue. The couple, who love to host, wanted the evening to feel like a night at their home with speeches added in. “Of course, Micah and I decided it was necessary to make our way around dinner, taking a shot with every single table,” says Zana. “Needless to say, the energy escalated pretty quickly. Everyone loosened up, we ate incredible food, laughed all night, and had the absolute best time.”

However, the night didn’t end just yet. The couple and friends piled into golf carts back to their villa. “The second I walked through the door, my 22-pound dress hit the floor, and everyone jumped straight into the pool in their clothes. I opted for slightly less clothing and did a little skinny-dipping,” says Zana. “My mom and dad came out of bed and jumped in wearing their pajamas, while my brother and the rest of our family were mildly appalled that I was completely naked. It was chaotic and ridiculous and absolutely perfect.” She adds, “It will forever be one of my favorite memories from the weekend.”

The ceremony took place the next day on the black sand beach surrounded by lava rock and cliffs overlooking the ocean. “It was dramatic. It was raw. It was perfect,” describes Zana. The bride walked down the aisle with her father to “Somewhere Over the Rainbow,” and Micah’s best friend Evan Enriques officiated the proceedings. “The vows were, without question, the heart of it all,” remembers the bride. “There was nothing gentle or lighthearted about them. They were genuine and from the heart—raw and unfiltered, just like the place where we stood. From what we’ve heard since the wedding, there wasn’t a dry eye in sight.” The couple both felt as if everything else fell away and they were speaking to each other from the heart. “It was one of the best moments of my life,” says the bride.

The reception kicked off with cocktail hour, followed by dinner and dancing. “Micah’s seven-year-old niece opened dinner with a prayer in ʻŌlelo Hawaiʻi, which was such a special way to begin the evening,” says Zana. Speeches were followed by a hula performance by Micah’s three sisters and niece, then a fire knife dance from the groom’s best friend, Larry “Tui” Tuileta. “Before long, Micah and Evan had joined him,” says Zana. Watching the three of them together was so special because this wasn’t something created for the wedding—they have been doing versions of this at family parties since they were little.”

“The rest of the night is honestly a blur in the best possible way,” says the bride. Dancing was followed by another late-night jump into the pool at the villa after-party. “Eventually, it was just Micah and me and a handful of our closest friends sitting around the dinner table, talking until four in the morning. A couple of them stayed so late that they left the table and headed almost directly to the airport for their flights home.”

“It felt like the perfect way to end the weekend,” adds the bride. “We’re just heartbroken that we can’t do it all over again!”

Exactly one year before our welcome party, Micah and I were legally married at Kona Village, just the two of us. It felt only right to rewear the stunning Hanne Bloch silk tulle two-piece set I wore that day. I’m so glad I did. It was such a special way to bring a piece of that intimate day into our wedding weekend. —Zana

It’s happening! I remember walking up to the Moana Lawn and thinking, “Oh my gosh, it’s really here.” Seeing everything I had envisioned come to life brought this incredible combination of relief and excitement. Suddenly, it was all real. —Zana

I wanted our welcome flowers to be inspired by the plumeria flower lei so often given upon arriving in Hawaiʻi. To make this vision come to life, our florist, Ren MacDonald-Balasia, went down to Kealakekua and met with a very special retired gardener who let her cut and purchase blooms directly from her yard. She had the longest oncidium orchids growing out of the lava rock wall that were about 36 inches a stem. She used them like vines and wove them through the butter yellow shower-tree blooms to create an unexpected arrangement of yellow en masse—intentionally combined together to invoke curiosity, like it could be one flower, not two. —Zana

My grandma and one of my best friends, hand-in-hand and cocktail in hand. Exactly the spirit we were hoping for all weekend! —Zana

This photo captures the pure joy I felt watching all of my favorite people arrive for our wedding weekend. Savannah is my childhood best friend, and I had the privilege of standing beside her during her own magical wedding celebrations. Now it was my turn. There is something so special about moving through life’s biggest chapters alongside the people who have known you the longest. —Zana

In nearly every childhood photo I have with my mom, I’m holding on tight. She’s always meant the world to me. Living overseas means I don’t get to hug her nearly as often as I’d like, so when I do, I never take it for granted. —Micah

Are you kidding?! The sunset, the people, the weather, the place, and THAT MAN! No words will ever do it justice. —Zana

In this moment, I remember feeling exactly the way I used to in college while watching Micah play volleyball at UCLA. His charisma and energy are unlike anything I’ve ever experienced, and I think everyone there was completely charmed by him in that moment. It was just so perfectly Micah. —Zana

This photo captures my wife perfectly. Her joy, her spirit, and her enthusiasm for life. —Micah

My niece has been asking her mom nonstop if she can please go back to Uncle Micah and Aunty Zana’s wedding. I’m not sure anyone had a better time than she did. —Micah

Everyone hard at work putting together their scouting reports.

Obviously, Micah won pickleball. And no, nobody took it easy on him. —Zana

For our save-the-dates, I embroidered our wedding details onto the same linen my dress was made from. They simply read, “Micah and Susannah – Kona Village, HI – May 24, 2026.” My Grandma Sue, never one to miss an opportunity, used hers to customize her hat for the pickleball tournament. —Zana

I’m pretty sure I didn’t stop smiling the entire weekend! —Zana

We’re a competitive bunch, so naturally, we had to hire legitimate referees for our pickleball tournament. —Micah

The long farm tables, the warmth of the fire, and the soft lighting made the evening feel less like a formal rehearsal dinner and more like a family dinner in our own home.

We wanted the florals to feel like a celebration of Hawaiʻi. Our florist Ren sourced rare bromeliad blooms that were punctuated by ripe and shiny mountain apples that were sourced from the Hilo farmer’s market. She wanted the arrangements to invoke a sense of lava flowing through the rocks, so in addition to the fiery color palette, she used hala lei made from the pandanus fruit to slope down the actual lava rocks at the base of the piece.

Hand in hand, on our way to the rehearsal dinner. —Micah

My beautiful mother made a special lei from naupaka, the flower we had chosen as the symbol of our wedding. —Micah

My two younger sisters gave such an amazing speech, starting the night off in a way that made it feel like one big family dinner. People reminisced about old times and our stories became even grander than the last time we had told them. —Micah

My relationship with my sisters has never been a rollercoaster full of highs and lows. Instead, for as long as I can remember, it has been a steady source of the most loyal and loving support that I have experienced. —Micah

I feel like one of the luckiest people in the world to have parents who have supported every dream I’ve ever had. My wedding was no exception. Watching my dad beam as he saw me living out my fairy-tale wedding meant everything to me. —Zana

I might be biased, but this was one of the best meals of my life! The warmth of the fire, the local vegetables, and a family-style dinner beneath the lights and trees. I’ll never get over it. —Zana

Our niece and goddaughter loved my Kilentar shell-and-fringe dress just as much as I did! I remember seeing it for the first time and thinking, “This isn’t a want. It’s a need!” —Zana

A wedding-morning canoe ride—just the two of us!

The ocean has always been such an important place for us. It’s a place of healing and a place of cleansing. Before we make a big move across the world or a big decision in life, we have always made sure to jump in the water. —Micah

She sells seashells by the seashore. And he buys them just to spend a little more time with her. —Micah

Growing up, The Parent Trap was my all-time favorite movie. There’s a scene at camp where they’re raising and lowering the flag that has always stuck with me. When we started dreaming up our wedding weekend, I wanted it to have that same nostalgic feeling of summer camp. And, of course, no summer camp would be complete without a flag. —Zana

Seeing my wedding dress hanging beside the mini dress made from my mother’s wedding gown was incredibly meaningful. My parents’ marriage is something I’ve always admired and aspired to, and having such a special piece of their wedding day woven into my own felt like a beautiful full-circle moment. —Zana

The most incredible human I’ve ever known. My mom. —Zana

From the moment Micah and I met, we shared the same greatest priority in life: our families. So when it came time to decide who I wanted around me while getting ready, the answer felt obvious. I wanted to be surrounded by the women who have shaped my life. They wore the most beautiful House of Pacific dresses, while I got ready in a Danielle Frankel robe. —Zana

The dramatic contrast of my billowing white Danielle Frankel gown against the jagged black lava still takes my breath away. —Zana

The two men who have lifted me up and carried me through every chapter of my life. —Zana

Moments before walking down the aisle. I was more nervous than I’d expected. I think the magnitude of what was about to happen finally caught up with me. —Zana

One of the greatest gifts God has ever given me is this man. My father. —Micah

I found this suit in an underground shop near Red Square in Moscow. The story is far too long to tell, as so many of our stories from living overseas tend to be. But getting married in Hawaiʻi wearing a suit I found in Russia just about sums up our lives. —Micah

Micah and I had originally chosen another ceremony location on the property, but the moment we saw this spot, we knew our plans had to change. The drama of the black lava against the crashing blue waves felt like the perfect setting for this chapter of our story. —Zana

We wanted the ceremony florals to feel as though they were growing naturally from the landscape, complementing the beauty of the island rather than competing with it. Our florist so beautifully juxtaposed the sharpness of local foraged Kona grasses with the softness of cream colored oncidium orchids. The grasses created waves while the orchids created fluttering foamy moments, indicative of the ocean behind the ceremony.

Our guests making their way to the ceremony.

I have dreamt of this moment hundreds of times since I was a little girl. I always imagined my dad would cry because, if you know him, you know he’s a big softie. But somehow, neither of us did. Instead, we laughed and smiled in complete disbelief at just how perfect everything felt. —Zana

I’ve never experienced a moment where I was so completely unaware of everything else happening in the world. Watching your future wife walk down the aisle is a feeling that can’t really be explained. It’s something you can only understand once you’ve experienced it. —Micah

Whenever someone asks me about my favorite moment of the weekend, I don’t have to think twice. It was sharing our vows. —Zana

There is no better feeling than knowing the people you love most absolutely adore the man you’re about to marry. —Zana

Smiles, tears, laughter, and so much love. This ceremony had it all.

In true Parent Trap fashion, we recessed down the aisle to Natalie Cole’s “This Will Be.”

Just two kids who fell in love and never looked back.

I asked Ren, our florist, for a cascading bouquet with just a hint of color and left everything else in her hands. As she did so many times throughout the weekend, she absolutely blew me away with what she created.

Micah’s hands have always been one of my favorite things about him. Seeing a wedding ring on his finger felt completely surreal. —Zana

A poolside cocktail hour overlooking the black lava and deep blue sea.

The brother of the bride clearly had no fun at all! —Zana

Round tables beneath the palms, soft white linens, and the ocean in the distance made for the most beautiful setting for dinner.

For the reception, Ren carried the natural beauty of the island through to our dinner tables. The tables were full of symbolism and native material. One of the most special symbols were the Naupaka branches and flowers, an ode to the Hawaiian legend of Naupaka and the symbol we chose to represent their wedding. There was also local gardenia from Oahu on every table, a very special flower to Micah’s family. The gardenia were hand carried on the plane, and the extra effort to bring them over was worth it as their fragrance wafted through the reception tables with each passing Kona breeze. —Zana

I’ve always loved making things—particularly embroidery and sewing—so I created these hardcover menus myself, embroidering each guest’s name onto the linen cover. —Zana

A bare statement piece that blends so seamlessly into the surrounding environment while still making a statement.

Quite possibly my favorite photo of Micah ever. —Zana

We both come from long lines of storytellers, so when someone in the family gets hold of a microphone, you know it’s showtime.

Aside from marrying the love of my life, this was the most emotional moment of the entire weekend for me. My sisters mean everything to me. It’s always been the four of us. They’ve danced hula since we were kids, and having them dance for us and—in their own way—bless our marriage was incredibly moving. It was the second time that day I cried. —Micah

My lifelong best friend has been fire-knife dancing at our family parties since we were eight years old. There was no way we could end our wedding night without him performing, just as he always has for us. He’s one of the most talented people I know, and man, can he spin those sticks! —Micah

Ending the night the only way we saw fit.

#6789. The 6 Winter Coat Trends Defining the Season

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

From sculptural tailoring to vintage-inspired faux fur, these are the styles to know

A great winter outfit deserves an equally great coat, especially when it’s an essential layer for the next several months. Beyond the practical need for warmth, outerwear often sets the tone for an entire look as the first layer you see. A sharply tailored wool coat can make jeans and a sweater feel more polished, while an oversize silhouette or rich texture brings dimension and new proportions to otherwise clean-lined looks.

For fall/winter 2026, designers are rethinking classic outerwear through distinctive silhouettes, textures, and details. At Ferragamo, Tory Burch, and Fendi, precise tailoring took a dressier turn, with slim silhouettes, tuxedo-inspired designs, and satin lapels bringing eveningwear polish to wool coats. Meanwhile, Ralph Lauren, Mugler, and Burberry embraced leather for a sleeker city-ready take on winter dressing. Faux fur took on a distinctly vintage feel at Stella McCartney, Bottega Veneta, and Khaite, while plush collars added texture to everything from elegant overcoats to more everyday designs.

Whether you’re looking to invest in a forever piece or simply want something fresher than the coat you’ve worn for the past few winters, these six trends offer plenty of inspiration.

Faux fur is taking a distinctly retro turn this winter, with plush textures and elegant silhouettes reminiscent of vintage finds. Stella McCartney’s floor-grazing belted coat and Bottega Veneta’s voluminous fur both recall the glamour of the ’30s and ’40s, while Khaite’s shaggy cream jacket has more of a ’70s feel, particularly when dressed down with jeans. Of course, we love a faux-fur coat as the finishing touch to a dressy outfit, but there’s something even chicer about pairing one with everyday denim and boots.

Arma Verena Reversible Shearling and Leather Coat

For fall/winter 2026, the black evening coat is having a moment. Designers showcased styles with luxe updates to keep things more interesting. Think sharp, menswear-inspired tailoring with a more formal finish, as seen at Celine, to elegant satin coats at Dries Van Noten. It’s the go-to coat to wear to upcoming holiday parties and formal dinners, or if you just want to upgrade your traditional winter coat for something a bit more luxurious this season.

Polo Ralph Lauren Wool and Silk Crepe Tuxedo Duster Coat

The Row Erdene Single-Breasted Wool Long Coat

There’s a certain refinement to a beautifully tailored coat, especially when the details borrow from formalwear. Think precise cuts, elongated silhouettes, and tuxedo-inspired touches that feel polished enough for an evening out. There’s a more dressed-up sensibility to these classic designs—as seen at Ferragamo, Tory Burch, and Fendi—from the precise fit to the smallest finishing details. This attention to detail brings a beautiful sense of sophistication to workwear and when paired with simple everyday separates.

Gap x Victoria Beckham Wool-Blend Chesterfield Coat

Mackage Elodie-R Double-Breasted Wool-Blend Coat

When a puffer or classic wool coat feels too predictable, a leather coat offers a much bolder alternative. Ralph Lauren, Mugler, and Burberry all embraced waist-defining silhouettes, from classic double-breasted trenches to softer robe-like shapes. In dramatic maxi lengths, the effect is especially sleek, with just the right amount of edge, bringing a bit of bite to winter dressing.

Nili Lotan Arsene Leather Double-Breasted Trench Coat

The Frankie Shop Edra Shearling-Trimmed Wrap Coat

Gray was ubiquitous on runways from New York to Paris, appearing in everything from textured tweed to draped wool and sharply tailored shapes. Whether you prefer deep charcoal or soft dove, it’s an easy neutral to wear in tonal layers or to balance bright colors and prints.

Banana Republic Herringbone Wool-Blend Top Coat

Marant Etoile Pilda Herringbone Double-Breasted Coat

’S Max Mara Scarf-Detail Virgin-Wool Wrap Coat

Faux fur was all over the fall/winter 2026 runways, even in smaller doses like plush collars. If you know that feeling of a sharp chill hitting your neck when the rest of you is bundled up, these collars offer the warmth you need in an ultra-elegant way. On everything from sporty puffers and classic toggle-front wool coats, as seen at Louis Vuitton, to the patterned and pretty pastel trims at Chanel and Gabriela Hearst, it’s a detail that’s as practical as it is beautiful.

Max Mara Medusa Belted Puffer Coat with Faux-Fur Trim

#6787. No More Franchises

No more prequels. No more reboots. No more Harry Styles in Eternals. No more of these 71 other things.

No more movie franchises. No more shared universes. No more post-credits scenes. No more prequels. No more reboots. No more eight-hour streaming TV spin-offs. No more slates and phases. No more multiverses. No more crossovers.

No more movies that are only made to greenlight sequels. No more sequels made for getting you to sign up for a streamer that raises its monthly subscription price every year. No more Easter eggs. No more winks. No more fourth-wall breaks. No more action scenes that halt the story and are clearly directed by the second unit. No more teasers that lead to nothing. No more Harry Styles in Eternals. No more watch guides and chronological order explainers and breakdowns. No more asking, “Is it canon?”

No more four-quadrant tentpoles. No more movies based on kids’ stuff that my niece can’t actually watch. No more Superman movies that are so violent and destructive that they trigger my 9/11 survivor mother’s PTSD. No more R-rated films that sell Funkos. No more movies that have to appeal to foreign markets and all the meemaws and pawpaws in Idaho. No more quippy dialogue where characters remark, “Well, THAT just happened!” No more irony. No more grotesque violence set to upbeat pop songs. No more characters looking into their own phones. No more thudding exposition, and especially not in the first ten minutes. No more “no more romances.”

No more hiring interesting up-and-coming filmmakers with buzz coming out of Sundance and Telluride because they’re cheap and have credibility to exploit. No more boxing in those same artistes because they’ll say “yes” to all marching orders. No more rejecting established auteurs with an interesting pitch and a desire to play in the sandbox because it doesn’t fit into next summer’s tentpole. No more prioritizing release dates over craft and the well-being of everyone working on it.

No more geriatric thespians putting on spandex because today’s adult moviegoer refuses to grow up themselves. No more casting red-hot twenty-somethings and locking them into seven-movie contracts. No more firing those actors because they got into legal trouble so the audience gets gaslit into forgetting there was ever something called The Kang Dynasty. No more international talent getting nothing cool to do; no more Hiroyuki Sanada getting killed by Jeremy Renner in Avengers: Endgame. No more casting directors deciding based on their exact amount of Instagram followers. No more content creators getting cameos.

No more Comic-Con. Or rather, no more making Comic-Con into Coachella. No more sleeping on the sidewalks for a seat in Hall H. No more buzzy presentations that turn art and myth into product reveals. No more “we’re doing it for the fans” and “one more thing.” No more Oscar winners promoting movies that don’t even have a script. No more actors lying through their teeth about how they read the original comics growing up. No more trailers that shake the room for those who slept outside to get in, and then get uploaded to YouTube while they collect their sleeping bags.

No more press screenings with ridiculous embargoes. No more taking away my phone and stuffing it into a zip pouch because of a spoiler that heaven forbid leaks on TikTok when millions were spent making it in front of IMAX cameras and a unionized crew; no more thinking any of this is tantamount to government secrets. No more influencers on red carpets. No more junket “interviews” that are just quizzes and games. No more gushing. No more unprofessionalism.

No more studios that exist only to adapt in-house IP. No more C-suites rambling about the lucrative potential in old cartoons and ‘90s comic books like old-timey oil barons surveying land. No more touting the box office of one movie as evidence why they oughta make a dozen more. No more pretenses about the power of stories in earnings calls with Merrill Lynch. No more forgetting, and not giving healthy royalties to, the comic book creators whose imaginations filled the calendar slate and fueled the stock prices in the first place.

No more toxic fandoms. No more powerful studios kowtowing to the loudest, most obnoxious YouTubers who make a living screaming into microphones in their basements. No more chuds who bemoan wokeness in whatever the latest remake/sequel they’re supposed to be mad about, and use AI-generated thumbnails of themselves making the dumbest fucking faces with cherry-picked unflattering screenshots of actresses who wouldn’t give them the time of day anyway. No more abusers, sex pests, misogynists, and racists anywhere, let alone in charge.

No more ten-year plans. No more stoking tuckered-out fans to drum up excitement about the next Batman or James Bond. No more actors keeping up action figure physiques while they wait years to hear about the sequel. No more taking characters and stories people have spent their lives escaping into for comfort and deforming them into numbers on a spreadsheet. No more vague bullshit like “It didn’t capture the zeitgeist” to explain why you’re arm-swiping everything off the table again. No more using the word “zeitgeist” if you cannot define it without ChatGPT.

No more cowardice. No more promises no one can keep. No more of this circus. No more.
